sections.h2: Choosing how to sell in Greenfield
sections.html:
Anyone selling a Greenfield house picks among an agent listing, a sale handled alone, and a cash purchase of the house in its present state. The city sits in Milwaukee County and counts 37,159 residents as of July 1, 2025, against 37,803 in the 2020 census.

Listing makes sense for an updated house when you can sit through weeks of showings. A direct sale fits a dated kitchen, postponed repairs, a vacant property or an estate that needs settling. Both paths finish at the same place, the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds, with the same fee and return.

Just over half of Greenfield households own. The citywide middle value is a midpoint, so a house with original systems and finishes usually sells under it.

sections.h2: Who buys and who sells here
sections.html:
Many Greenfield owners stay a long time. Around 89.2 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier, and 37.6 percent of households are one person living alone. Original kitchens, bathrooms and mechanical systems are therefore common. Of 18,035 housing units, 3.8 percent stood vacant, and the homeowner vacancy rate was 0.9 percent.

Milwaukee winters are cold and wet, so buyers look hard at the roof, sump pump and furnace. Receipts showing recent service help, and you should have them ready for the first showing or the first conversation with a direct buyer.

sections.h2: Questions for the city before you list
sections.html:
Start with the City of Greenfield's building inspection office. Ask whether any permit on the property remains open, and whether an addition, finished basement or deck ever received its final inspection. Open permits can come up when a buyer digs into the file and can slow down a conventional sale. A direct buyer will usually take the file as it stands, though you still want the answer.

  • Building, electrical or plumbing permits that lack a final inspection.
  • City orders about the outside of the property, such as a fence or accessory building.
  • Special assessments for street or utility work that appear on the tax bill.
  • Whether tenants live in the house and on what terms.

The same office can say which repairs need a permit if you plan to fix things before selling.

Because Greenfield lies in Milwaukee County, the deed is recorded at the Milwaukee County Register of Deeds, 901 N. 9th Street, Room 103, Milwaukee. The office is open from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays, records and indexes real estate documents, and collects the real estate transfer tax. The seller owes 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction thereof under Wis. Stat. 77.22.

A Greenfield closing generally moves through four stages:

  • Order title work and ask your lender for a payoff letter.
  • File the electronic transfer return with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.
  • Record the deed at the Register of Deeds in downtown Milwaukee.
  • Receive your proceeds after liens and prorated taxes are paid.

The statute carves out exceptions. Transfers by will, descent or survivorship, transfers from parent to child for nominal consideration, and foreclosure deeds to the mortgage holder owe no fee (Wis. Stat. 77.25). Milwaukee County also offers a free Property Fraud Alert, which notifies a registered owner whenever their exact name shows up as grantor or grantee on a recorded document. It can be useful to anyone who still owns other real estate.

Sellers of one-to-four unit property have 10 days after accepting a contract to deliver a completed Real Estate Condition Report. When it is late, the buyer may rescind during the two business days after the tenth day and take the deposit back (Wis. Stat. 709.02). A personal representative, trustee or similar court-supervised fiduciary who never lived there is excused.

Before you fill it out, walk the house and note what you know about the basement, roof, plumbing and wiring. Each known problem has a place on the form, and honest answers protect you after closing.

Wisconsin real estate tax is normally payable in two equal parts, January 31 and July 31. A municipality may instead authorize three or more installments by ordinance, with at least half due by April 30 and the rest by July 31 (Wis. Stat. 74.11 and 74.12). The next due date is January 31, 2027.

The City of Greenfield treasurer can tell you what remains unpaid, which lets the title company prorate the bill between you and the buyer. Settle any balance you can before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: Fix it first or sell as is?
sections.html:
Whether to repair is up to you. The condition report still has to list the defects you know about. A buyer who purchases as is takes the work on, which can save an owner both money and the headache of hiring contractors.

Get a quote for large items such as a roof or furnace and compare it with the price gap between a repaired house and an untouched one. If the numbers look close, a cash sale gives you a firm date and removes the wait for showings and loan approval. Sellers dealing with an estate often find that a quick, as-is sale is simpler than managing repairs for a house they no longer live in.

faqs.q: Which county records a Greenfield, WI deed?
faqs.a: Milwaukee County. Take it to the Register of Deeds at 901 N. 9th Street, Room 103, Milwaukee, which records real estate documents and collects the transfer tax.

faqs.q: What is the transfer fee for a Greenfield sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction thereof. Transfers by will or descent and some family transfers are exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25.

faqs.q: What should I check with the city before listing in Greenfield?
faqs.a: Ask the building inspection office about open permits, exterior orders, special assessments and tenant occupancy. Clearing or disclosing them early avoids surprises in a buyer's review.

faqs.q: Must I repair a Greenfield house before I sell?
faqs.a: No, repairs are your choice. The condition report still has to disclose defects you are aware of, and an as-is buyer takes on the work.

faqs.q: When is Greenfield property tax due?
faqs.a: January 31 and July 31 in two equal installments, unless the municipality has authorized three or more by ordinance. The city treasurer can give you the exact amount and dates on your bill.
